claims.text: Demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Willingness to buy on its own is not demand: demand is effective when buyers are also able to pay the price, so a want without the ability to pay stays outside demand.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is sometimes confused with supply: demand refers to the quantities buyers are willing and able to take at each price, whereas supply, developed in topic 2.4, refers to the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer; the test is which side of the market the quantity belongs to.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The relationship between a good's price and the quantity demanded is inverse: as the price rises, the quantity demanded tends to fall, and as the price falls, the quantity demanded tends to rise, where nothing else changes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A demand schedule lists the quantities demanded at each of a series of prices, and a demand curve draws the same relationship with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, sloping downward from left to right.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity, while quantity demanded is the amount bought at one single price; a change in the good's own price shows as a movement along the demand curve, not a shift of the curve: a fall in price causes an extension of demand and a rise in price a contraction of demand.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Price and quantity are sometimes mixed up on the axes of a demand diagram: price belongs on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, and the test is that a movement along the curve then shows a price change leading to a quantity change, not the reverse.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Individual demand is the quantity of a good that one consumer is willing and able to buy at each price, and market demand is the quantity that all the consumers in a market together are willing and able to buy at each price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Market demand at each price is found by adding together the quantities that every individual consumer demands at that price, working price by price through the schedule.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: If one Oshakati household demands 4 litres of milk a week at N$10 a litre, a second demands 6 litres at the same price, and the rest of the market demands 90 litres, market demand at N$10 a litre is 100 litres a week.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The conditions of demand are the influences on demand other than the good's own price, including consumers' incomes, the prices of substitutes and complements, tastes and preferences, expectations of future prices, and the number of consumers in the market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A change in a condition of demand shifts the whole demand curve: an increase in demand shifts the curve to the right, meaning that at every price consumers are willing and able to buy more, and a decrease in demand shifts it to the left.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Substitutes are goods that replace one another in use, so a rise in the price of one tends to raise demand for the other, while complements are goods used together, so a rise in the price of one tends to lower demand for the other.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The test for a movement or a shift is whether the good's own price changed: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, whereas a change in a condition of demand shifts the whole curve.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where consumers expect a good's price to rise in future, demand for it tends to increase now, as they buy before the rise; where they expect the price to fall, current demand tends to decrease as they wait.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in the number of consumers in a market, through population growth, people moving into the area or a change in the age make-up of the population, tends to increase market demand at every price, shifting the market demand curve to the right; a fall in their number tends to decrease it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
